desc:
Each interval [start, end) is half-open: it covers every moment t with start ≤ t < end. Two intervals overlap when some moment is covered by both; intervals that merely touch (one ends exactly where the other starts) do not overlap.

Count the unordered pairs of different intervals (different positions in the list) that overlap. Identical intervals count as separate ones.

intervals = [[1, 4], [2, 6], [5, 8]]  ->  2

The first two overlap and the last two overlap, but the first and the last do not.
hints: Testing all pairs is O(n2), too slow for 50,000 intervals. Count the pairs differently: group them by the interval that starts later.
Sort the intervals by start. For the i-th interval in that order, an earlier one overlaps it exactly when it has not ended by the time the i-th starts.
Among the i earlier intervals, those that ended are the intervals with end ≤ start_i. Count them with a binary search in the sorted list of all ends, and add i - ended.
editorial: Two intervals overlap exactly when the one that starts later (ties: either) starts before the other one ends. So walk through the intervals in order of start; the pairs formed with earlier-starting intervals are the earlier intervals that are still active at this start.

Every interval with end ≤ start_i began strictly before start_i, so it is among the first i intervals in sorted order. Therefore the number of active earlier intervals is i - (number of ends ≤ start_i), and the number of ends is found by binary search in the sorted array of ends. Summing over i gives the answer in O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
Equivalently you can sweep events and add the current number of active intervals every time a new one starts.
solution:
from bisect import bisect_right


def countOverlappingPairs(intervals):
    starts = sorted(s for s, e in intervals)
    ends = sorted(e for s, e in intervals)
    total = 0
    for i, s in enumerate(starts):
        total += i - bisect_right(ends, s)
    return total
